section: 8. Roads (road element UML, after the t_road attribute table)
caption: Figure 33. UML Model for Roads
shows: UML class diagram of t_road: attributes name[0..1], length (t_grZero, >0), id (string), junction (string), rule (e_trafficRule [0..1]). Children with multiplicities: link 0..1, lanes exactly 1, objects 0..1, signals 0..1, railroad 0..1, type 0..* (t_road_type: s, type, country[0..1]; with speed 0..1 -> max, unit), surface 0..1, lateralProfile 0..1, elevationProfile 0..1, planView exactly 1. Also lists e_countryCode variants (alpha2 current; alpha3 and old codes deprecated) and t_maxSpeed = t_grEqZero or e_maxSpeedString.
lesson: Every road needs exactly one planView and exactly one lanes element; everything else is optional. junction is mandatory as an attribute (use "-1" when not a connecting road). length must be strictly positive. Road type entries are a sequence keyed by s, each may carry one speed child.
right: Always emit <planView> and <lanes> per road
Always write junction="-1" for normal roads
Use ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes on <type>
Write <type s=..> entries in ascending s, speed as child of type
wrong: Omitting <lanes> or <planView> - multiplicity 1 means schema-invalid
Writing length=0 for degenerate OSM ways - t_grZero forbids it; drop or merge zero-length segments
Using alpha-3 country codes - deprecated in 1.7

section: 8. Roads / 8.3 Road reference line geometry (UML for planView, lateralProfile, elevationProfile, surface)
caption: Figure 34. UML model for Road Geometry
shows: UML: planView has 1..* geometry (s, x, y, hdg, length>0) each holding exactly one of line / spiral(curvStart, curvEnd) / arc(curvature) / poly3(a..d, deprecated) / paramPoly3(aU..dU, aV..dV, pRange). lateralProfile has 0..* superelevation(s,a,b,c,d) and 0..* shape(s,t,a,b,c,d). elevationProfile has 0..* elevation(s,a,b,c,d). surface has 0..* CRG(file, sStart, sEnd, orientation, mode, purpose, sOffset, tOffset, zOffset, zScale, hOffset).
lesson: Geometry, elevation, superelevation and shape are all piecewise cubic records keyed by s (shape additionally by t). A geometry record carries its own start pose (x,y,hdg) and length; there is no implicit chaining - the writer must make poses consistent.
right: Emit at least one <geometry>; each with exactly one primitive child
Shape records need both s and t
paramPoly3 needs pRange (arcLength or normalized)
wrong: Emitting poly3 for new data - deprecated; prefer paramPoly3
Computing geometry s values that do not equal the accumulated sum of previous lengths - consumers rely on contiguous s

caption: Figure 35. Allowed, prohibited, and recommended road linkage
shows: Four panels, each two roads with lanes 1 (yellow, left of reference line) and -1 (blue, right), blue arrow = reference line direction. Top-left: reference lines do not touch (gap) - red X. Top-right: the first reference line runs past the start of the second (overlap) - red X. Bottom-left: reference lines meet exactly at one point but the roads have a heading kink, so the lane areas show a gap on the outer side and an overlap on the inner side - yellow warning triangle (allowed, not recommended). Bottom-right: roads join with a common point and common tangent, lanes flush - green tick (recommended).
lesson: Linked roads must share the endpoint of their reference lines exactly (G0). Tangent continuity (G1) is recommended; a heading kink is tolerated but produces lane gap/overlap wedges.
right: End point of predecessor reference line == start point of successor reference line
Same heading at the joint so lane polygons are flush
wrong: Reference line gap between linked roads - prohibited
Reference line overlap (one road extends past the other's start) - prohibited
Heading kink at the joint - allowed but creates lane gaps/overlaps; avoid by smoothing OSM polylines into G1 geometry

caption: Figure 36. Allowed scenarios of road linkage
shows: Four panels with Road 1 (left) and Road 2 (right), lanes labelled per road. (a) Both reference lines run left-to-right: Road1 successor = 2 contactPoint start; Road2 predecessor = 1 contactPoint end. (b) Road 1 reference line points left (its lane -1 is on top, 1 below), Road 2 points right: both STARTS meet; Road1 predecessor = 2 start, Road2 predecessor = 1 start; successors n.a. (c) Road 1 points right, Road 2 points left (Road2 lane -1 on top, 1 below): both ENDS meet; Road1 successor = 2 end, Road2 successor = 1 end. (d) Red X: Road 1 has lanes 2,1,-1 with its reference line drawn between lanes 2 and 1, Road 2 has lanes 2,1,-1 with reference line between 1 and -1 - the two reference lines are laterally displaced at the joint, so they do not connect.
lesson: Predecessor/successor is about the START/END of the road's own reference line, and contactPoint says which END of the other road touches. Opposite-direction roads can be linked directly (start-start or end-end); lane ids flip sign across such a joint because left/right swap. Reference lines must coincide at the joint; you cannot compensate a lateral jump of the reference line by renumbering lanes.
right: Head-to-tail: succ contactPoint=start / pred contactPoint=end
Start-to-start: both use predecessor, contactPoint=start
End-to-end: both use successor, contactPoint=end
If OSM way directions oppose, keep the roads and link with matching contact points instead of reversing geometry
wrong: Assuming successor always has contactPoint=start
Linking roads whose reference lines are laterally offset at the joint (e.g. reference line on a different lane boundary) - not a valid link; use a laneOffset to move lanes, or a junction
Leaving out the reciprocal link on the other road (the tables always fill both roads)

caption: Figure 37. Allowed scenario of road linkage within a junction
shows: An incoming road with lanes -1 and -2 (one direction, arrows right) enters a dashed junction box. Inside are two connecting roads: one curving up-right carrying a single lane -1 starting from incoming lane -1, and one straight carrying lane -1 starting from incoming lane -2. The straight connecting road continues into an outgoing road with one lane -1. Each connecting road has its own reference line starting exactly at the incoming road's endpoint area.
lesson: When one road splits into several, the split must be modelled as a junction with one connecting road per path; each connecting road has its own reference line, can carry a subset of lanes and renumbers them from its own centre lane (incoming -2 becomes -1 on the straight connector).
right: Use a junction for one-to-many road splits
Connecting roads carry only the lanes needed for that path and number them from their own centre (-1, -2, ...)
Connecting road reference line starts on the incoming road's end cross-section
wrong: Linking one road directly to two successor roads without a junction - road link is 1:1
Copying incoming lane ids into the connector (lane -2 kept as -2 with an empty -1)

caption: Figure 38. UML model for road linkage
shows: UML: t_road_link has predecessor 0..1 and successor 0..1 of type t_road_link_predecessorSuccessor with elementId (required), elementType (road/junction), contactPoint [0..1], elementS [0..1], elementDir [0..1].
lesson: A road has at most one predecessor and one successor. contactPoint is optional in the schema but required in practice when elementType=road (and absent when linking to a junction, which uses no contact point); elementS/elementDir are only for virtual junctions.
right: elementType=road -> give contactPoint
elementType=junction -> elementId=junction id, no contactPoint
wrong: Emitting more than one <successor> for a road
Using elementS/elementDir for ordinary road-road links

caption: Figure 39. Types of elevation
shows: Three panels. Road Elevation: a curve h(s) in the s-z plane, h measured vertically, local frame (s,t) moved along. Super Elevation: cross-section in the t-z plane; the road surface is rolled about the reference line (point s), h' is the rotated normal - elevation along t. Road Shape: cross-section with t positive to the LEFT; piecewise linear profile with widths 1 m, 4 m, 3 m, 1 m between t=5, 4, 0, -3, -4; h=0.05 m at t=5..4, h=0.45 m at t=0 (reference line peak), h=0 at t=-3..-4; slopes b=-0.10 m/m and b=0.15 m/m.
lesson: Three independent height mechanisms: elevation (function of s), superelevation (roll angle about the reference line, function of s), shape (height offset as function of t, at given s). They add up.
right: Elevation for longitudinal grade from OSM/DEM
Superelevation for banking
Shape only for non-planar cross-sections (crown, crossfall)
wrong: Encoding crossfall as elevation or lane height
Treating shape t-axis as positive to the right - it is positive to the left as for all t

caption: Figure 40. Superelevation
shows: Cross-section in x-z with t pointing left. Left: a=0, road flat, a point at lateral distance t1 lies at horizontal distance t1. Right: a>0, road surface rotated about the reference point s so the left side rises; the point at t1 along the tilted surface projects horizontally to t1*cos(a); h axis is tilted with the surface.
lesson: Superelevation is a pure rotation about the reference line: lane widths are measured along the tilted surface, so the plan-view footprint shrinks to t*cos(a) and the left edge rises by t*sin(a). Positive roll raises the left (positive t) side.
right: Measure lane widths along the rolled surface
Positive superelevation lifts the +t (left) side
wrong: Assuming plan-view (x,y) width stays equal to lane width under superelevation
Sign-flipping the roll angle (positive = right side down)
formula: x_offset = t*cos(a); z = h_ref + t*sin(a); a(ds) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3 (radians)

caption: Figure 41. Minimum t-definition range for road shapes
shows: Plan view of a road (lanes 4..1 left, -1..-3 right) whose outer borders narrow along s. Two lateral profiles at s_R1 and s_R2 (red vertical lines); red circles mark the t-start of each shape polynomial: five at s_R1, three at s_R2, and each profile spans the full road width from outer left to outer right border (green bracket = minimum t range = maximum t extent of the whole road). A point (s_P, t_P) lies between the two profiles. Formulas: h_SR1(t_P) and h_SR2(t_P) = a + b*dt + c*dt^2 + d*dt^3, and h(s_P) printed as (h_SR1(t_P) + h_SR2(t_P))*(s_P - s_R1)/(s_R2 - s_R1).
lesson: Each shape profile must cover the maximum t extent of the entire road, not only the local width; heights between profiles are interpolated linearly in s; within a profile, dt is measured from that polynomial's own t start.
right: Every s-profile covers t from the widest right edge to the widest left edge of the road
Linear interpolation along s between profiles
Profiles can have different numbers of polynomials
wrong: Defining shape only over the local road width - points elsewhere become undefined
Taking the printed formula literally: (h1+h2)*(sP-sR1)/(sR2-sR1) does not give h1 at sP=sR1; implement proper linear interpolation
formula: h(s_P,t_P) = h_R1(t_P) + (h_R2(t_P) - h_R1(t_P))*(s_P - s_R1)/(s_R2 - s_R1); h_Ri(t) = a + b*dt + c*dt^2 + d*dt^3 with dt = t - t_start(polynomial). Figure prints (h_R1+h_R2)*(s_P-s_R1)/(s_R2-s_R1), which looks like a typo.

caption: Figure 42. Shape definition (left) in combination with superelevation (right)
shows: Same cross-section as Figure 40 but with a grey shape profile on top of the road (height rising toward +t). Left a=0: shape added vertically on a flat road. Right a>0: road rolled, the shape is applied perpendicular to the tilted surface (along tilted h), point t1 projects to t1*cos(a).
lesson: Shape heights are applied in the superelevated (rolled) frame: shape is evaluated in t along the tilted surface and offset along the rolled h axis; superelevation is applied first, shape on top.
right: Compute shape in the local rolled frame
wrong: Adding shape height to global z after superelevation as if unrolled

caption: Figure 43. Road surface as defined in a CRG file
shows: 3D rendering of a road surface with cobblestone (paving block) texture in one half and a smooth section with a pothole in the other, white dashed centre marking, kerbs on both sides - surface relief from a CRG file.
lesson: OpenCRG supplies fine-grained surface relief (cobbles, potholes) on top of the OpenDRIVE road; it is not a substitute for lane geometry.
right: Reference CRG via <surface><CRG> only if real surface data exists
wrong: Trying to model surface relief with elevation/shape polynomials

caption: Figure 44. ASAM OpenCRG road surface description using u/v-coordinates and x/y-coordinates
shows: Plots of a sample CRG file (belgian block): XY overview of the CRG reference line (a curve from about (226,84) to (234,78)); XYZ height map in curved XY grid (z about 2.04-2.18 m); UVZ map in an uncurved grid, u = 730..740 m along the line, v = -1.5..1.5 m across.
lesson: CRG has its own reference line and its own (u,v) coordinates, analogous to OpenDRIVE (s,t); combining requires a mapping between the two.
right: Treat u~s, v~t with offsets
wrong: Assuming CRG u starts at 0 or aligns with road s=0

caption: Figure 45. Positioning of an ASAM OpenCRG file along the reference line
shows: OpenDRIVE road in s/t (yellow +t, blue -t). A CRG grid placed from s_Start to s_End; the CRG reference line (black arrow) is offset below the road reference line by t_Offset.
lesson: The CRG patch is valid only over [sStart, sEnd] and its reference line may be laterally shifted by tOffset relative to the road reference line.
right: Set sStart/sEnd to the CRG extent
wrong: Assuming the CRG reference line coincides with the road reference line

caption: Figure 46. ASAM OpenCRG attachment mode, attached
shows: Mode attached: CRG grid with its u/v axes placed parallel to the road s/t axes, origin shifted by sOffset and tOffset; the CRG reference line is discarded and the patch bends with the OpenDRIVE reference line.
lesson: In attached mode CRG (u,v) are simply (s - sOffset, t - tOffset); CRG heights are added to the OpenDRIVE height.
right: Use attached when surface detail should follow the OpenDRIVE geometry
wrong: Using CRG XY geometry in attached mode
formula: u = s - sOffset; v = t - tOffset; z = crg(u,v)*zScale + zOffset + h_OpenDRIVE(s,t)

caption: Figure 47. ASAM OpenCRG attached mode with elevation
shows: Longitudinal profile: blue reference line elevation rising between sStart and sEnd; the CRG data (dark band) starts at sOffset and rides on top of the OpenDRIVE elevation.
lesson: In attached mode the CRG relief is superimposed on the road elevation; heights outside the CRG data range are plain OpenDRIVE.
right: Total height = OpenDRIVE height + CRG delta

caption: Figure 48. ASAM OpenCRG attached0 mode with elevated reference line
shows: Same profile in attached0 mode: OpenDRIVE elevation is set to zero (red line at z=0) inside [sStart,sEnd]; CRG data supplies the absolute height from sOffset; between the end of CRG data and sEnd there is a hatched region where height falls to z=0 - a gap.
lesson: In attached0 the OpenDRIVE elevation is ignored, so sStart/sEnd must match the CRG data boundaries exactly or the surface drops to zero.
right: sStart/sEnd exactly equal to CRG data extent
wrong: sEnd beyond CRG data in attached0 - produces z=0 holes

caption: Figure 49. ASAM OpenCRG attachment mode, genuine
shows: Mode genuine: CRG u/v axes rotated by hOffset relative to s/t and placed at (sOffset, tOffset); the CRG reference line (u) keeps its own curvature, not following s.
lesson: In genuine mode the CRG geometry is used as-is relative to the start point (translated and rotated by hOffset); it does not bend with the OpenDRIVE reference line.
right: Use genuine for measured surfaces with their own geometry
wrong: Expecting genuine CRG to follow road curvature

caption: Figure 50. ASAM OpenCRG orientation
shows: Top: orientation=same, CRG grid corners A,B,C,D, origin (u=0,v=0) at sStart offset by tOffset, u along +s, v along +t. Bottom: orientation=opposite, grid rotated 180 deg (corner letters upside-down), u (labelled n) points to -s and v to -t; tOffset is shown on the other side.
lesson: orientation=opposite is a 180 deg rotation about the CRG origin: both u and v reverse sign relative to s and t.
right: Flip both u and v for opposite
wrong: Flipping only u (mirror) - text matrix [[0,-1],[-1,0]] swaps axes; the figure shows a plain 180 deg rotation
formula: opposite: u = -(s - sOffset), v = -(t - tOffset) (as drawn)

section: 8.6.1 Modeling a road shape with a linear crossfall
caption: Figure 51. Example crossfall modeled with road shape
shows: Cross-section with t positive to the LEFT. Profile: flat h=0.05 m from t=5 to t=4 (width 1 m); slope down from h=0.45 m at t=0 to 0.05 at t=4 (width 4 m, b=-0.10 m/m); from h=0 at t=-3 rising to 0.45 at t=0 (width 3 m, b=0.15 m/m); flat h=0 from t=-4 to -3 (width 1 m). Table of four shape records all at s=0: t=4 a=0.05 b=0; t=0 a=0.45 b=-0.1; t=-3 a=0 b=0.15; t=-4 a=0 b=0.
lesson: Each shape record is valid from its own t to the next larger t, and is evaluated with dt = t - t_record in the +t direction. Hence slope on the -t side is POSITIVE (0.15) because the profile rises towards the reference line when moving in +t.
right: Shape records sorted by t ascending at each s; dt measured from the record's t
One s value can hold several t-records forming a piecewise polynomial
wrong: Writing b with the visual slope sign (seen left-to-right in the drawing) - sign must refer to increasing t
Evaluating dt from t=0 instead of the record's t start
formula: h(t) = a + b*(t - t_i) + c*(t - t_i)^2 + d*(t - t_i)^3 for t_i <= t < t_{i+1}

caption: Figure 52. Center lane for road with lanes of different driving directions
shows: Two-way road: lanes 3,2,1 above (yellow, left) and -1,-2 below (blue, right); centre lane 0 drawn as dash-dot line coinciding with the road reference line (no lane offset). At a vertical section boundary a new right lane -3 appears: the dashed boundary -1/-2 stays straight, a NEW dashed line peels off from it to the outer side and the solid outer edge swings outward, so the new lane opens with zero width next to lane -1; the old outer lane keeps its width and is now numbered -3 (labels -1, -2, -3 in the second part). Lane 3 on the left is separated by a solid line (e.g. shoulder).
lesson: Lane ids are always contiguous from the centre lane (1,2,3 / -1,-2,-3) inside each lane section; when a lane is inserted the ids of all lanes outside it shift by one in the new section. Centre lane has no width; without laneOffset it equals the reference line.
right: Renumber lanes in each section consecutively from the centre
Link old -2 -> new -3, old -1 -> new -1; the new (zero-width-start) -2 has no predecessor
wrong: Keeping the old id for the continuing outer lane and giving the new lane id -3 when it is geometrically between -1 and the old -2
Linking the opening lane to old -2

caption: Figure 53. Center lane for road with lanes of identical driving direction
shows: One-way road: only left lanes 1, 2 (driving, arrows pointing AGAINST the reference line direction, i.e. leftwards) and 3 (separated by solid line), centre lane 0 on the reference line at the right edge of the road; no right lanes.
lesson: A one-way road may consist of only one side; the centre lane then lies on the road edge. With right-hand traffic, left lanes are driven opposite to the reference line - so a one-way road built only of left lanes runs against s.
right: One-way: use only right lanes (traffic along +s in RHT), or only left lanes with traffic in -s
Centre lane at road edge is fine
wrong: Putting a one-way OSM way's lanes on the left side while expecting traffic in +s direction

caption: Figure 54. UML model for lanes
shows: UML: lanes has laneOffset 0..* (s,a,b,c,d) and laneSection 1..* (s, singleSide[0..1]). laneSection has center exactly 1, left 0..1, right 0..1; each holds lane 1..* with id = 0 (center), positiveInteger (left), negativeInteger (right). All lanes (lr) have type, level[0..1], link 0..1 (predecessor 0..*, successor 0..*, each with integer id), geometry 1..* via width 0..* or border 0..*, plus height, material, speed, access, roadMark, rule (all 0..*).
lesson: Lane link predecessor/successor are 0..* - multiple are allowed (splits/merges). A lane needs width or border (one of them). Center lane is mandatory in every section and carries only roadMark/link, no width.
right: Emit <center><lane id=0> in every laneSection
Use multiple <predecessor>/<successor> only for abrupt split/merge
wrong: Omitting center
Giving the center lane a width
Mixing width and border in the same lane group

caption: Figure 55. Lane grouping with left, center, right
shows: Road with left group (lanes 3, 2, 1 with arrows pointing left), centre (lane 0 dash-dot on reference line), right group (lanes -1 arrow pointing right, -2). Lane 3 and -2 separated by solid lines (non-driving).
lesson: Positive ids are left of the centre lane, negative right; under right-hand traffic right lanes drive along +s and left lanes along -s, so direction is derivable from the id sign (except bidirectional).
right: Order lanes in XML from left to right (descending id)
Direction from id sign + road rule
wrong: Placing forward-direction lanes of an RHT road on the left side

caption: Figure 56. A road section with lane sections
shows: Lane section A: lanes 3,2,1 | 0 | -1,-2. Lane section B: a new lane opens at the CENTRE side: a dashed line peels off from the reference line and swings out, the former -1/-2 solid boundary and the outer edge also swing out in parallel; at the end of B the lanes are -1 (new, inner), -2 (former -1), -3 (former -2). Left lanes unchanged.
lesson: A change in lane count needs a new lane section, and the new lane starts with zero width at the section start. Because ids count outward from the centre, a lane appearing near the centre renumbers every outer lane on that side.
right: New section at the s where the new lane begins (width 0)
Links: A:-1 -> B:-2, A:-2 -> B:-3; B:-1 has no predecessor
Left side lanes link 1->1, 2->2, 3->3
wrong: Matching lanes across sections by id instead of by position
Giving the zero-width-start lane a predecessor

caption: Figure 57. Lane sections defined separately for both sides of the road
shows: Left side: lane section A_left ends where a narrowing left lane (solid outer border tapering onto the dashed line) has disappeared, B_left starts at that s. Right side: section boundary A_right/B_right lies further downstream, where an outer right lane tapers (solid border rising onto the dashed/solid boundary). Boundaries on the two sides are at different s.
lesson: With singleSide=true a lane section can apply to one side only, so lane count changes on left and right sides need not force a common section boundary.
right: Use singleSide sections when left/right lane changes occur at different s, or split both sides at every change (equivalent, more sections)
wrong: Assuming singleSide is required - a full section split at each change is also valid
Ending a lane section before the tapering lane reaches zero width

caption: Figure 58. Lane offset
shows: Section A: lanes 3,2,1 | 0 on reference line | -1,-2. Section B: the centre lane (dotted line) rises smoothly from the reference line to the former 1/2 boundary (lane offset growing); lane 1 shrinks to zero above it while a new lane -1 grows below it, so labels read 3,2,1,0,-1,-2,-3. Section C: lanes 2,1 | 0 (offset from reference line by constant 'Lane offset') | -1,-2,-3; reference line itself unchanged.
lesson: laneOffset moves the centre lane laterally; lanes may move from left to right side (e.g. a centre turn lane), which changes the lane count per side and requires new lane sections. Lanes outside keep their geometry but get new ids.
right: Use laneOffset (not reference line changes) to shift the lane split for turn lanes/asymmetric widening
Links A:2->C:1, A:3->C:2, A:-1->C:-2, A:-2->C:-3, A:1 shrinks to 0 (no successor at zero width), new -1 starts at 0 width
wrong: Combining laneOffset with lane borders - forbidden
Using a non-linear laneOffset together with road shape - inconsistent
Linking a lane that ends with zero width to a successor
formula: t_center(s) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3, ds = s - s_laneOffset

caption: Figure 59. Lane links for road with id 10
shows: Three roads in a row. Road 30 and Road 10: reference lines pointing right, lanes 1 above, 0, -1, -2 below. Road 20: reference line pointing LEFT (arrow at its left/start-of-view end, i.e. its end touches road 10's end), lanes -1 above, 0, 1, 2 below. The dashed lane boundary lies at the same height across all three. Table: road 10 lane 1: pred 1 (road 30), succ -1 (road 20); lane -1: pred -1 (30), succ 1 (20); lane -2: pred -2 (30), succ 2 (20).
lesson: Lane predecessor/successor refer to the start/end of the lane's own section in its own s-direction, independent of driving direction. When the next road is reversed (end-to-end contact), the linked lane ids flip sign, and the link points into the last lane section of that road.
right: Lane succ on road 10 refers to ids of road 20's section at contact point (end -> last section)
Negate ids across opposite-direction road joints
wrong: Copying the same id across an opposite-direction joint
Swapping predecessor/successor based on traffic direction
Pointing into road 20's first section when contactPoint=end

caption: Figure 60. Example where a bikeway ends and bicycles are expected to continue driving on the driving lane
shows: Top view: multi-lane carriageway; at the bottom a red bikeway with bike symbol and arrow in s direction, separated from the adjacent driving lane by a white line; the bikeway ends abruptly (non-zero width) mid-image, beyond which the asphalt of the adjacent lane covers the former bikeway area.
lesson: When a lane ends abruptly with non-zero width and its users continue on a neighbouring lane, link it with a successor to that neighbour; the neighbour then has two predecessors (itself and the bikeway).
right: bikeway.successor = driving lane of next section; driving lane next section has 2 predecessors
wrong: Leaving an abruptly ending bikeway unlinked
Tapering an abrupt end to zero width just to avoid multi-links

caption: Figure 61. Example where a driving lane splits into two or more driving lanes abruptly
shows: Top view: a single wide lane (no centre marking) suddenly becomes two lanes at a visible section boundary: a dashed divider starts there; the upper new lane has an arrow straight-then-left, the lower straight-then-right, both in +s direction. Outer solid edge lines continue unchanged.
lesson: An abrupt split of one lane into two (both non-zero width at the boundary) is modelled with one lane having two successors (and each new lane the same predecessor).
right: wide lane: successor ids of both new lanes; both new lanes: predecessor = wide lane
wrong: Using multi-successors when a new lane opens gradually beside a continuing lane - then only the continuing lane is linked

caption: Figure 62. UML Model t_road_lanes_laneSection_lcr_lane_link
shows: UML: lr_lane (level, type) has link 0..1; link has predecessor 0..* and successor 0..*, each with integer id.
lesson: Link ids are plain integers pointing into the neighbouring lane section (same road) or the first/last section of the linked road per contactPoint; multiplicity allows split/merge.
right: Omit <link> only when lane ends in a junction or has no physical continuation
wrong: Writing road id or lane section index in a lane link - only lane id

caption: Figure 63. UML model lane properties
shows: UML: LaneGeometry 1..* realised by width 0..* (sOffset,a,b,c,d) or border 0..* (sOffset,a,b,c,d); height 0..* (sOffset, inner, outer).
lesson: Lane shape is given either by width polynomials or by border polynomials, keyed by sOffset relative to the lane section start.
right: sOffset relative to the lane section s
wrong: Using absolute s as sOffset

caption: Figure 64. Change of lane width per lane section
shows: Section A: lanes 1 | -1, ds1 starts at section A start; lane -1 constant width (a=const, b=c=d=0). Section B: ds2 restarts at section B start; a new outer lane -2 widens from 0 (a=0, b,c,d widen it) to full width. Outer solid border moves to the outer edge of -2; the -1/-2 boundary is unmarked at first and gets a dashed mark only once -2 has grown wide.
lesson: Width polynomial ds restarts at 0 at each width element (sOffset relative to section). A newly opening outer lane starts with a=0. Width is measured from the inner border, so outer lanes stack on inner ones. Road marks along the new boundary can start later via roadMark sOffset (none, then broken).
right: New lane: width a=0 at section start
Solid outer edge mark belongs to the outermost lane (move it to -2)
roadMark type none until lane is usable, then broken
wrong: Evaluating ds from road s=0 or from section start when sOffset>0
Keeping the solid edge mark on lane -1 after -2 appears
Starting new lane with full width (abrupt step)
formula: width(ds) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3; s = s_section + sOffset + ds

caption: Figure 65. Lane with varying border shape
shows: Same geometry as Figure 64 modelled with borders: green arrows from the reference line to each outer border. Section A: border of -1 a=const, b=c=d=0. Section B: border of -1 const; border of -2 starts with a_-2 = a_-1 (coincident, zero width) and b,c,d move it outward; at the end a_-2 const.
lesson: Borders are absolute t-offsets of a lane's OUTER edge from the reference line (not from the neighbour); a zero-width lane has border equal to its inner neighbour's border.
right: Border value = signed t of outer edge (negative on right)
No laneOffset when borders are used
Borders must not cross
wrong: Treating border as width
Mixing width and border in the same side group

caption: Figure 66. Lane types for a motorway
shows: Motorway cross-section, left to right: shoulder (grass, with reference line arrow running along its left outer area), border, three driving lanes (dashed separators), stop (hard shoulder, brown), shoulder (green), none.
lesson: Motorway pattern: driving lanes flanked by border/shoulder on the inside and stop (emergency lane) plus shoulder on the outside; 'none' for area outside the road.
right: Hard shoulder = stop, not shoulder
Use border for the narrow strip next to the median barrier
wrong: Labelling the emergency lane as shoulder or driving

caption: Figure 67. Lane types for a rural road
shows: Rural road: none, shoulder, driving, restricted (yellow-hatched wedge widening between the two opposite driving lanes), driving, shoulder, none.
lesson: Hatched painted islands between opposing lanes are lanes of type restricted with varying width (starting at zero).
right: restricted lane with polynomial width for hatched islands
wrong: Modelling a painted island as a gap or as median

caption: Figure 68. Lane types for an urban road
shows: Urban road, left to right: border, curb, driving, driving, curb, median (grass), curb, driving, driving, border, curb, parking (paved bays with varying width), shoulder (grass whose width complements the parking bays), biking (red, arrow +s), sidewalk.
lesson: Curbs are their own narrow lanes; medians are separate lanes bounded by curbs; parking bays are a parking lane with varying width with an adjacent shoulder taking up the complement so outer lanes stay straight.
right: Explicit curb lanes next to medians and sidewalks
Varying parking width + complementary shoulder width
wrong: Folding curbs into sidewalk width
Ending the parking lane between bays instead of letting its width vary

caption: Figure 69. Lane types for motorway exit and entry
shows: Top view of a dual carriageway with three driving lanes per direction. Upper carriageway: an exit lane (brown) next to driving lanes, then a short block labelled offRamp still parallel to the motorway, then the offRamp road curving away. Lower: an onRamp road curves in, a short parallel onRamp block, then an entry lane (green) alongside the driving lanes.
lesson: Lane type along a ramp changes: exit (deceleration) -> offRamp at the divergence; onRamp -> entry (acceleration) at the merge. The parallel stretch next to the motorway belongs to the motorway with type exit/entry, then a short transitional section with ramp type, then the ramp road.
right: Link exit lane -> offRamp lane (type change is a valid linkage case)
entry lane starts where the onRamp lane joins
wrong: Typing the deceleration lane as offRamp or driving
Leaving the type change unlinked

caption: Figure 70. Lane types for motorway connecting to another motorway
shows: Same layout as Figure 69 but between two motorways: ramps labelled connectingRamp (incl. the short parallel block) while the parallel lanes are still exit and entry.
lesson: Motorway-to-motorway ramps use connectingRamp; exit/entry still apply to the lanes beside the main carriageway.
right: connectingRamp for motorway interchanges
wrong: Using offRamp/onRamp for motorway-motorway links

caption: Figure 71. Lane-specific speed limits
shows: Road with left lanes 1 (80), 2 (60), 3 and right lanes -1 (80), -2. Speed signs on left lanes are drawn upside-down (read from the -s driving direction); arrows: left lanes leftward, right lane rightward.
lesson: Speed limits can differ per lane and per direction; lane speed overrides road type speed (signals still have preference).
right: <speed> per lane with sOffset; centre lane none
wrong: Assuming one speed for the whole road when OSM gives maxspeed:lanes or :forward/:backward

caption: Figure 72. Lane access, bus lane
shows: Same road: lane 2 (left, driving direction leftward) marked 'Bus' (bus-only), lanes 1 and -1 ordinary.
lesson: Access restrictions are per lane (<access> rule allow/deny restriction=bus).
right: access rule=allow restriction=bus for bus lanes (others then banned)
wrong: Encoding bus lanes only via lane type

caption: Figure 73. Lane height
shows: Cross-section with t positive to the left: lanes 4..1 left, -1..-4 right; car on -3; pedestrian on lane -4 raised by 'lane height' above the road surface; lane 4 also raised (orange); lane width marked.
lesson: Lane height lifts a lane (sidewalk/curb) by a small offset relative to the road surface (including elevation, superelevation, shape); inner and outer heights can differ.
right: height inner/outer ~0.12-0.15 for sidewalks
wrong: Using lane height for road grade
Raising the centre lane

caption: Figure 74. Lanes excluded from road elevation
shows: Superelevated cross-section (tilted, h axis rotated): lanes 3..1, -1..-3 follow the tilt; outermost lanes 4 and -4 are crossed out and drawn horizontal (level), each continuing at the height of the adjacent inner lane's outer edge; -4 additionally has a lane height (raised sidewalk).
lesson: level=true lanes ignore superelevation AND shape, staying horizontal at the height of the inner neighbouring lane's edge.
right: level=true for sidewalks/curbs on banked roads
Several consecutive outer lanes may be level
wrong: Applying level to inner lanes
Expecting level lanes to keep the road crown/crossfall

caption: Figure 75. UML model t_road_lanes_laneSection_lcr_lane_roadMark
shows: UML roadMark: sOffset, type, color, weight[0..1], width[0..1], height[0..1], material[0..1], laneChange[0..1]; children sway 0..* (ds,a,b,c,d), type 0..1 (name, width; line 1..* with length, space, tOffset, sOffset, rule, width, color), explicit 0..1 (line 1..*: length, sOffset, tOffset, rule, width).
lesson: Road marks belong to a lane (its outer border; centre lane mark is the centre line), keyed by sOffset; detailed patterns via type/line, irregular ones via explicit, lateral wiggle via sway.
right: Put the centre line mark on lane 0, edge marks on outermost lanes
laneChange to express crossing permission
wrong: Putting a mark on both lanes sharing a border (double marks)

caption: Figure 76. Road marking with sway and offset
shows: 3D view of a motorway construction zone: yellow temporary lines defining the actual driving lanes swerve across the permanent white markings; red-white beacons along them.
lesson: sway lets a road mark deviate laterally from its lane border without changing lane geometry (marks-only shift, e.g. construction sites).
right: Use sway when the paint deviates but lane topology does not
wrong: Changing lane widths just to move paint
formula: t_mark = t_border + sway(ds), sway(ds) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3
